items.title: NBA Teams Get Tougher On Star Extensions: 'Being Unhappy Is Not A Negotiating Position Anymore'
items.summary: NBA teams are taking a tougher approach with star players who want contract extensions. This offseason, the New York Knicks, Washington Wizards and Detroit Pistons all refused to give in to unhappy stars. "A year or two ago, I don't think you'd have seen that," said an Eastern Conference executive. "The teams would've felt too much pressure. Being unhappy is not a negotiating position anymore." Karl-Anthony Towns said publicly that he wanted an extension and would accept less than a maximum contract. The Knicks issued a statement ending talks, and Towns started the season unhappy. Towns holds a $61 million player option for 2027-28 and could become an unrestricted free agent next summer. Anthony Davis also wanted an extension with the Wizards and can opt out next summer. Agent Rich Paul made it known that Davis would take less than a max deal. But the Wizards put talks on hold to see how the first 20 to 30 games go, ESPN's Shams Charania reported. Davis then said he would wait until after the season. Jalen Duren, coming off All-Star and All-NBA selections, agreed on the eve of training camp to a $200 million deal with Detroit, $87 million less than his maximum. Other teams went the opposite way showing the power that the NBA's true superstars continue to wield. The Los Angeles Lakers sent two first-round picks and two pick swaps to the Utah Jazz in a sign-and-trade for Walker Kessler, giving him a four-year, $130 million contract. The Lakers had promised Luka Doncic a rim-running big man and the 2026 offseason was their best opportunity to acquire one due to their vanishing cap space. The Minnesota Timberwolves rebuilt their roster largely to please Anthony Edwards. Edwards wanted to play shooting guard and pair with LaMelo Ball. Both teams hope to sign their stars to extensions next summer. A Western Conference general manager said unhappiness still works for top stars, as he pointed to Giannis Antetokounmpo, who left the Milwaukee Bucks without publicly demanding a trade. "He actually did them a favor," said the GM. "He gave them a list of five teams. He could have given them only one." Another West GM said the second apron gives teams more reason to say no. "I know the fans are tired of hearing about the aprons, but this is just another example of how they are changing the league," said the GM. "The aprons give the owners a reason to take a harder line. Before, it was just about money." The lasting power of the trend lasts may depend on how the Towns and Davis situations play out over the next few months for the Knicks and the Wizards.

items.title: 76ers-Knicks Sets Opening Night Record With 7.71M Viewers
items.summary: Tuesday's NBA opening night doubleheader on NBC and Peacock averaged 6.41 million viewers, the most-watched opening night in league history. The Philadelphia 76ers' 106-100 win over the New York Knicks averaged 7.71 million viewers. It was the most-watched primetime opening night game ever and peaked at 9.1 million viewers at 9:45 p.m. ET. Philadelphia spoiled ring night for the defending champion Knicks. It was the 76ers' first game since signing LeBron James and trading for Jaylen Brown this offseason. The second game was a rematch of last season's Western Conference finals as the Oklahoma City Thunder beat the San Antonio Spurs by a final score of 116-104.

items.title: Olympiacos Pursuing John Konchar
items.summary: EuroLeague power Olympiacos is pursuing veteran NBA wing John Konchar. Olympiacos is looking for reinforcements on the perimeter after some recent turbulence with their roster. Konchar was signed to a training camp deal with the New York Knicks. The 6-foot-5 guard/forward was considered a favorite to land an opening night spot, but was waive near the start of camp to attend to a personal issue. Olympiacos lost wing Shaquielle McKissic in the offseason. Then veteran wing Evan Fournier suffered a sprained MCL in his right knee and a bruised shoulder. On top of those absences, guard Tyler Dorsey was suspended by the Greek club after complaining publicly about his role and contract. There had been speculation that Konchar could land with another NBA team later in the season. Several teams are carrying open roster spots, but a handful won't be able to fill them until they're deeper into the season due to lack of room under a incurred hard cap.

items.title: NBA Generated $14.5 Billion In Revenue Last Season, Led By Warriors' $895M
items.summary: The NBA generated approximately $14.5 billion in revenue during the 2025-26 season. The 30 teams brought in a combined $13.7 billion, an average of $456 million each, with the rest kept at the league level. The Golden State Warriors led all teams with $895 million in revenue. The Memphis Grizzlies ranked last at $339 million. The totals are after revenue sharing, which moved about $400 million to lower-revenue teams. The NBA's 11-year, $76 billion media deal raised each team's national TV payout from $103 million to $144 million last season. Those payments will rise by approximately seven percent a year on average. Central league revenue made up 41 percent of team revenue. Seating and luxury suites brought in an estimated $3.64 billion. The Warriors led the league with nearly $5.5 million in ticket revenue per game, and the Los Angeles Lakers and New York Knicks each topped $4 million. The Knicks' playoff run generated $180 million in gross revenue. Sponsorships totaled $1.9 billion. Golden State's sponsorship revenue was about $190 million and should top $200 million this season with a new jersey patch deal worth more than $50 million a year. Local media revenue is expected to drop this season after Main Street Sports' bankruptcy affected 13 teams. The Lakers have the NBA's biggest local TV deal, worth about $200 million a year with Spectrum. The average NBA franchise is now worth $6.64 billion, up 21 percent from last year. If Las Vegas and Seattle both join the league, each existing owner would receive more than $500 million in expansion fees, which are not shared with players. The league has said it will decide on expansion by the end of the calendar year.
